thread.title: New report shows mismatch between home listings and buyers' incomes persists in U.S. market
thread.title_full: New report shows mismatch between home listings and buyers' incomes persists in U.S. market

author: Prairie State Wire
title: New report shows mismatch between home listings and buyers' incomes persists in U.S. market
text:
Households in the United States have access to about one-quarter fewer homes than they would in a balanced housing market, according to a May 20 joint report from the National Association of Realtors and Realtor.com.
The report introduces the Listing-Income Alignment Score, which measures how well home listings match local income distributions. A score of 100% means that listings are proportionally available across all income levels, while lower scores indicate that homes are concentrated at higher price points and less accessible for entry-level or middle-income buyers.
In March, the national Listing-Income Alignment Score reached 74.9%, an increase from 66.7% a year earlier but still below the pre-pandemic level of 84.4%. “Housing supply is growing and affordability is improving. However, the U.S. housing market continues to face a structural mismatch between the homes available for sale and what buyers can afford,” said NAR Principal Economist and Director of Real Estate Research Nadia Evangelou. “Too much of the inventory available today remains concentrated at higher price points, leaving a shortage of options for entry-level and middle-income buyers. This is preventing home sales from reaching pre-pandemic levels.” Middle-income households—earning about $75,000 per year—can currently access only about 23% of listings nationwide; ideally they would be able to access around 44%. The country needs roughly 311,000 more homes priced under $261,000 to reach balance.
“The improvement in our Listing-Income Alignment Score over the past year is encouraging, but the data makes clear that more inventory alone won’t be enough to unlock the housing market,” said Danielle Hale, Chief Economist at Realtor.com. “A true recovery requires homes at the right price points. Until the supply of entry-level and middle-market homes grows to meet demand, many buyers will continue to find the market out of reach despite headline improvements in affordability and inventory.” The Midwest has some of most aligned markets: Toledo (107.4%), St. Louis (106%), Akron (105%), Pittsburgh (102.6%), and Detroit (102.4%). In contrast, Los Angeles (39.4%) and San Diego (45%) are among those with greatest mismatches.
Nearly all major metro areas improved or held steady over last year; Madison was an exception with its alignment dropping nearly eight percentage points to 63%. Markets such as Lakeland (+18 percentage points), McAllen (+14.7), Las Vegas (+14), New Orleans (+13.2), and Cape Coral-Fort Myers (+13) saw notable gains after rapid pandemic-era price growth.
The National Association of Realtors supports diversity within real estate professions; it encompasses approximately 1,200 local boards as well as state associations; empowers professionals on property rights issues; delivers research resources including statistics and advocacy efforts; functions as a leading trade association for real estate practitioners; maintains headquarters in Chicago with another office in Washington D.C., according to the official website .

However, the U.S. housing market continues to face a structural mismatch between the homes available for sale and what buyers can afford,” said NAR Principal Economist and Director of Real Estate Research Nadia Evangelou.
